objectives.en: Read and say the five number stems — एक, द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च — every final sound intact, and pair each with its digit १–५ within a beat.
objectives.hi: पाँचों संख्या-मूल — एक, द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च — हर अन्तिम ध्वनि समेत पढ़ें-बोलें, और हर मूल को उसके अंक १–५ से एक ताल के भीतर जोड़ें।

objectives.hi: गिनती-घोष एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च सम ताल पर बोलें, चित्रों की वस्तुएँ उसी से गिनें, और हर गिनती घोष के अन्तिम शब्द पर पूरी करें।

objectives.en: State the honest two-dress line — stems are the citation names, the chant is the neuter counting dress, the full system waits for Volume 4 — and the no-arrow cognate shelf, including एक's honestly empty slot.

sections.name: Hook
sections.markdown:
You have been able to *read* पञ्च for a whole volume — it carried the ञ्च showcase — and
to *write* ९ since the signs lesson. What you could not yet do, in the language whose
grammarians counted everything, is count. v1.c06.l01 left a promise on the record: the
names of the numbers beyond पञ्च are Volume 2 Chapter 3's business. Chapter 3 is here.
Today the first five numbers get their names — three old friends back on duty, two new
words older than every calendar they ever landed on, and one honest surprise: the word
for "one" has no clean English twin — *one* is a relative only at the root — and this
course will be the one to tell you.

sections.name: Previous Lesson Review
sections.markdown:
पुनरावृत्तिः — Station 0 first: Chapter 2's clock comes due today. Then four memory
prompts, everything from memory *before* any key opens [REF:roediger2006].

### Station 0 — the family-world exam's +1-week arrives

v2.c02.l05 §20 scheduled this week's re-runs: its tasks C and D, compressed. Three
minutes; log both scores beside the exam's [REF:cepeda2006].

1. **The family tree, one take** (task C, compressed): present four members in the
   frames — एषः/एषा matched to each person, एतत् for गृहम्, names via मम or the simple
   repeat. Pause form, every visarga breathed.
2. **Three direction cards, from memory** (task D, compressed) — keep or reject, one
   reasoning line each: (a) "English *mother* comes from Sanskrit मातृ." (b) "दुहिता
   and *daughter* are cognates." (c) "और is the Sanskrit for 'and'."

### The prompts

1. From v1.c05.l03: the number word that entered the ledger with the द्व ligature —
   and which *neighbor* did its §13 cognate note set beside it?
2. From v1.c06.l01: the five-word and its conjunct showcase — which stack welds inside
   it, and why is "panch" flagged?
3. From v1.c05.l05: write the digits १–५ from memory — and state the standing digit
   policy for this book's pages.
4. From v2.c02.l02: the pointing kit — three pointers, each matched to what you point at. Which
   one will run today's card game?

<details><summary>उत्तराणि · Answers</summary>

0. Station 0: tree = four lines with एषः/एषा correctly matched, pause form. Cards:
   (a) **reject** — siblings, no arrow between cousins; (b) **keep**; (c) **reject** —
   और is Hindi; Sanskrit's joiner is च (v2.c02.l05 §19 keys). Score /7; log it.
1. द्वि (dvi) "two" — its §13 note set त्रि beside it: द्वि ~ *two/duo*, त्रि ~
   *three/trēs*. Readable ever since, but a mention, not a headword — until today (§14).
2. पञ्च (pañca) — the ञ्च stack: a full consonant ञ on च's own station. "Panch" swaps
   it for a Hindi-style nasalized vowel (v1.c06.l01 §12).
3. १ २ ३ ४ ५ — Latin digits in prose; Devanagari digits as *content* when taught
   (v1.c05.l05, STYLE_GUIDE §3). Today they are content.
4. एषः for a man or boy · एषा for a woman or girl · एतत् for a thing — एतत् runs today's card
   game: एतत् किम्?
</details>

A dropped card or a flipped direction sends you to v2.c02.l05 §22's remediation row
tonight — not to a halt today.

sections.name: Historical Context
sections.markdown:
ऐतिहासिकः सन्दर्भः — the second-oldest drawer in the vocabulary, and a promise kept.

Last chapter opened the deepest drawer of inherited words — the kin terms. The numerals
live in the drawer beside it: learned in childhood, used daily, replaced almost never —
which is why the cognate shelf can open again today with full confidence.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** The stems एक, द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च are the numbers' citation
> names — the shapes this course teaches first and dictionaries list (पञ्च is headed by its
> full stem पञ्चन् (pañcan), whose final न् drops in compounds and in the counting form). In
> running Sanskrit, numbers *inflect*: they change dress by gender and case. The neuter
> counting recitation — एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च — is standard practice, real
> inflected Sanskrit learned whole. [REF:apte1890]; [REF:whitney1889]

One line of course history, stated as the salvage it is: the 1.x numbers unit (PDF
pp.30–31) taught the correct stems — the audit kept them — then attached a derivation
story about English month names that is not true. Today the stems arrive with labels on
and the shelf built honestly; the printed fix is next lesson's centerpiece. And a
smaller promise redeemed: v1.c06.l01 taught पञ्च as "a reading word that happens to be
the best count-race shout in the language" and pointed here. Here we are.

sections.name: Scientific Explanation
sections.markdown:
वैज्ञानिकं विवरणम् — why a chant, why a ladder, and why the beat matters.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** Number names are the textbook case for automaticity: a digit's
> name must arrive without translation, or counting stays a classroom trick. Timed
> retrieval of small chunks — today's beat-paced digit-name ladder — is the fluency
> strand doing exactly its job. [REF:nation2013]

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** Spaced retrieval beats massed re-study; today's Station 0 is
> v2.c02.l05's +1-week interval landing on schedule, and this lesson sets its own
> +1-day and +1-week re-runs before it ends (§20). [REF:cepeda2006] [REF:roediger2006]

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** Numerals are among the most stable items of basic vocabulary —
> rarely borrowed, slowly replaced. That stability is why they preserve the systematic
> sound-correspondences that serve as evidence of shared descent, and why the numeral
> set is a classic showcase of the Indo-European family's unity. [REF:mallory2006]

The chant earns its place twice: rhythm chunks a sequence for serial recall, and the
chant is real language data — learned whole now, understood as a system later
[REF:nation2013].

sections.name: Sanskrit Explanation
sections.markdown:
संस्कृतेन विवरणम् — counting, in sentences and half-sentences you fully own:

> **एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च।**
> (ekam dve trīṇi catvāri pañca.) "One, two, three, four, five." — एक, दो, तीन, चार, पाँच।

> **एतत् किम्? — त्रि!**
> (etat kim? — tri!) "What is this (card)? — Three!" — यह क्या है? — तीन!

> **पुष्पम् अत्र अस्ति। एकम्… द्वे… त्रीणि। — त्रीणि!**
> (puṣpam atra asti. ekam… dve… trīṇi. — trīṇi!) "A flower is here. One… two… three. —
> Three!" — फूल यहाँ है। एक… दो… तीन। — तीन!

Three moves, all old friends in new work: the chant counts while the finger points and
the count closes on its last chant word; the bare citation name answers a digit card;
and अस्ति keeps its standing job when something *is here*. No verb is needed: a digit
card answered bare — त्रि! — is this course's name-tag drill convention (§15), not a
full Sanskrit word. Pause form throughout, as always.

sections.name: Hindi Explanation
sections.markdown:
हिन्दी में समझिए

आज की सूची का आधा काम हिन्दी पहले ही कर चुकी है। एक तो वही का वही है; और दो, तीन, चार,
पाँच असल में द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च की ही सन्तानें हैं — सदियों की ध्वनि-यात्रा के बाद,
वैसे ही जैसे गृह चलते-चलते घर बना। दिशा का सच वही पुराना: हिन्दी संस्कृत की सन्तान है,
इसलिए यह दावा नीचे की ओर सच है; अंग्रेज़ी *two* और *three* बहनें हैं, बेटियाँ नहीं —
उनकी कहानी §13 की तालिका में है।

दूसरा — अन्त सँभालिए; आदतें यहीं फिसलती हैं। एक में अन्तिम अ पूरा बोलिए — हिन्दी की
आदत "एक्" कहकर रुक जाती है, संस्कृत का एक दो अक्षरों का पूरा शब्द है — ए की दो मात्राएँ, क की एक। चतुर् ठीक र् पर
रुकता है — उसके बाद कोई स्वर नहीं; हलन्त वहीं इसीलिए बैठा है। पञ्च में ञ पूरा व्यञ्जन
है — पाँच वाली चन्द्रबिन्दु-आदत यहाँ नहीं चलेगी (v1.c06.l01 की वही पुरानी चेतावनी)।
और त्रि की इ छोटी है — यह अंग्रेज़ी *tree* नहीं है।

तीसरा — दो वेश, एक ईमानदारी। एक, द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च शब्दों के *नाम* हैं — शब्दकोश
इन्हीं के नीचे इन्हें रखते हैं — बस पञ्च का शीर्ष-शब्द पूरा मूल पञ्चन् है। एकम्, द्वे, त्रीणि, चत्वारि गिनती की पोशाक है — सच्चा,
रूप बदला हुआ संस्कृत, जो आज पूरा घोष बनकर कण्ठ होता है। संख्याएँ लिंग और कारक के
अनुसार वेश बदलती हैं — वह पूरा तन्त्र Volume 4 में खुलेगा; तब तक गिनती घोष से, और
गिनती घोष के अन्तिम शब्द पर पूरी होती है — त्रीणि! अंक-कार्ड का उत्तर केवल नाम से — त्रि! —
यह इस पाठ्यक्रम की अभ्यास-परिपाटी है, पूरा संस्कृत पद नहीं। कोई नियम मत गढ़िए। और अंक १–५ (v1.c05.l05 की कमाई) आज
अपने नामों से जुड़ते हैं — कार्ड देखिए, एक ताल के भीतर नाम बोलिए।

sections.name: English Explanation
sections.markdown:
No new letter, no new sign — the standing Volume 2 luxury. The load is two ledger-new
words, three old friends back on duty, one chant, and one honest piece of bookkeeping.

### The set — five on duty

**एक** (eka) "one" — back from v1.c02.l04, the course's first number word, and the humblest headline of the day: say the whole word; the
Hindi habit clips it to "ek", and §12 is waiting. **द्वि** (dvi) "two" — back from
v1.c05.l03, where the द्व ligature made it readable. **त्रि** (tri) "three" — the
almost-old friend: mentioned in v1.c01.l01's cognate table and again in v1.c05.l03 §13,
readable for a volume, never a headword until today — so today it formally enters the
ledger (§14). **चतुर्** (catur) "four" — new, the course's first headword to *end on a
bare र्*: the tongue taps and the word stops, halanta and all. **पञ्च** (pañca) "five" — back
from v1.c06.l01, where it carried the ञ्च showcase and the promise this chapter keeps.

### Two dresses, honestly labeled

Each number owns two shapes today. The **stems** एक द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च are the
citation names — what the ladder answers, what a bare answer
uses. The **chant** एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च is the neuter counting dress — real,
inflected Sanskrit, the standard counting recitation, learned whole as a rhythm.
Numbers change dress by the gender and role of what they count; that system is honestly
deferred to Volume 4 (§15). Notice, for free, that पञ्च keeps one shape in both rows —
noticing is allowed, legislating is not.

### The digits pair up

१ २ ३ ४ ५ have been yours since v1.c05.l05; today they stop being mute shapes and get
their names. The ladder discipline (§9 drill 4, §18 exercise 1) runs both directions —
see the digit, say the name; hear the name, write the digit — within a beat each way.
The standing policy holds: Latin digits in prose, Devanagari digits as content.

### What is deliberately not here

The title एकादिपञ्चान्ताः (ekādipañcāntāḥ) "the ones from one to five" — एक and पञ्च
wearing their joined dress at the seams: एक + आदि "beginning with one", पञ्च + अन्ताः
"ending with five"; joining rules are Volume 3's business — read it, build nothing.

Three absences, all honest. The Sanskrit word that *asks* "how many?" is next lesson's
headword — today the pointing finger and the digit card ask the question. Numeral
agreement is Volume 4's machinery; today no number ever touches a plural noun (§15's
fence). And the shelf's एक slot stays empty: no clean everyday-English cognate, and the
course says so instead of reaching (§13).

sections.name: Pronunciation
sections.markdown:
उच्चारणम् — no new sounds; the work is full finals, dental onsets, and one word that
ends on a consonant. Audio: 🔊 `planned:assets/audio/volume-2/v2c03l01-drill.mp3`
(drills 1–3), `planned:assets/audio/volume-2/v2c03l01-word-list.mp3` (three speeds +
dictation track).

**Drill 1 — the finals.** एक in slow motion: long pure ए, then क with its *short full*
अ — three beats in all, ए two and क one. Then चतुर्: the tongue taps for र् and the word ends; if any
vowel escapes after the tap, re-run. Then पञ्च: pa — ñ — ca, the middle a full
consonant on च's station, never a nasalized vowel.

**Drill 2 — the roll-call.** With the audio, fixed order, three passes (slow · natural
· timed): एक — द्वि — त्रि — चतुर् — पञ्च. The order is the memory palace; your mouth
learns it so the ladder can shuffle it later.

**Drill 3 — the chant on a beat.** एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च — five words, five
beats, even tempo. The long vowels of त्रीणि and चत्वारि each take their two full
counts; keep the beat honest and the quantities take care of themselves. Then chant
while pointing: five fingers, five flowers on the worksheet, one word per touch.

**Drill 4 — the ladder.** The audio flashes digit calls; you name each within a beat:
३! — त्रि! Then the reverse row: hear *catur*, write ४. Log the third pass time (§18
exercise 1) — timed retrieval, the fluency strand on duty [REF:nation2013].

sections.name: IPA
sections.markdown:
No new values — every symbol has been on your chart since Volume 1.

**Word transcriptions (stems):** एक /eːkɐ/ · द्वि /d̪ʋi/ · त्रि /t̪ɾi/ · चतुर्
/t͡ɕɐt̪uɾ/ · पञ्च /pɐɲt͡ɕɐ/.

**The chant:** एकम् /eːkɐm/ · द्वे /d̪ʋeː/ · त्रीणि /t̪ɾiːɳi/ · चत्वारि /t͡ɕɐt̪ʋɑːɾi/ ·
पञ्च /pɐɲt͡ɕɐ/.

**Narrow notes.** एक opens on /eː/ — always long, a pure monophthong, never the English
"ay" glide [eɪ]; frozen-jaw test. त्रि: dental /t̪/ straight into the tap /ɾ/, one
gesture, then short /i/ — English *tree* fails it three ways (alveolar t, approximant
r, long vowel). चतुर्: opens on the palatal affricate /t͡ɕ/, carries a dental /t̪/
inside, ends on the bare tap /ɾ/ with no vowel after it; the chant form चत्वारि
[t͡ɕɐt̪.ʋɑː.ɾi] welds त्व with no seam vowel. त्रीणि hides a retroflex /ɳ/ after the
long /iː/ — tongue-tip curled, not dental न्.

sections.name: Mouth Position
sections.markdown:
मुखस्थितिः — four checks; the articulators know all of this already. The word-anatomy
strip on the digit-name cards (`planned:assets/images/volume-2/v2c03l01-digit-name-cards.svg`)
marks the त्रि and चतुर् joins.

1. **The frozen-jaw check.** Mirror on एक: set the jaw for ए and hold it still through
   the vowel — any drift toward "ay" means a diphthong leaked in. Then a full short अ.
2. **The teeth check.** त्रि and the त् inside चतुर्: tongue-tip *on the teeth*, not on
   the ridge behind them. English t is the ridge; Sanskrit त् is the teeth.
3. **The full-stop check.** Say चतुर् in slow motion and freeze on the last sound: the
   tongue taps and the mouth *holds* — no vowel escapes after the tap.
4. **The tongue-body check.** पञ्च: the middle of the tongue presses the palate for ञ —
   a held consonant, nose open — then releases into च. If the nose works alone and the
   tongue never lands, Hindi पाँच has intruded (v1.c06.l01's drill).

sections.name: Common Mistakes
sections.markdown:
सामान्याः भ्रान्तयः — real errors, each with its fix; these feed the quiz distractors.

1. **एक clipped to Hindi "ek".** The final अ is a real vowel and it is there. *Fix:*
   three beats — ए two, then a full /ɐ/ — the schwa-deletion discipline of Volume 1 never retires.
2. **चतुर् re-voweled to "chatura".** The halanta means what it says. *Fix:* §11 check
   3 — tap and stop, nothing after.
3. **पञ्च nasalized to "panch".** The v1.c06.l01 trap returns: Hindi पाँच replaces the
   full ञ with a nasalized vowel. *Fix:* tongue lands on च's station and holds a beat.
4. **त्रि stretched to English "tree".** Alveolar t, approximant r, long vowel — three
   errors in one syllable. *Fix:* dental त्, tap र्, short इ (§10, §11 check 2).
5. **The dress confusion.** Treating the chant forms as "the real numbers" and the
   stems as abbreviations — or the stems as correct and the chant as babytalk. *Fix:*
   both are real; different jobs (§15) — names versus counting dress.
6. **Agreement invented under enthusiasm.** Gluing endings onto numbers to make them
   "match" what is counted. *Fix:* the matching system is real and it is Volume 4's;
   today the chant counts, the bare stem answers a digit card, nothing is glued (§15's
   fence).

sections.name: Examples
sections.markdown:
उदाहरणानि — the shelf opens, one slot stays honestly empty, and a ledger debt is paid.

### The shelf — four sibling rows, no arrows

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** द्वि ~ Latin *duo* ~ English *two* · त्रि ~ Latin *trēs* ~ English
> *three* · चतुर् ~ Latin *quattuor* ~ English *four* · पञ्च ~ Greek *pénte* ~ English
> *five* — parallel descendants of the Proto-Indo-European numerals, among the most
> stable words in the family. No borrowing happened in any direction: nobody's "three"
> came from anybody else's. [REF:mallory2006]; [REF:burrow2001]

Read the shelf the way Chapter 2 taught you: no arrows between siblings. The tilde says
"same ancestor", and that is all it says.

### एक — the honestly empty slot

The shelf also teaches by what it *lacks*: एक has no clean everyday-English cognate to
put beside it. Etymological handbooks do trace एक and *one* to the same ancestral
root, but each language built its word with a different suffix — एक with a k, *one*
with an n — so they are relatives at the root, not the same inherited word the way
द्वि and *two* are [REF:mallory2006]. Printing them as a clean row would be reaching —
how the 1.x book went wrong — and honesty beats
reaching. The empty slot is itself the lesson: cognate rows are evidence, not
decoration, and where the evidence is not clean, this course says so out loud.

### त्रि — the word that was always almost here

त्रि has haunted this course since its first hour: v1.c01.l01's cognate table showed it
beside *three*, v1.c05.l03 §13 named it again beside द्वि — yet it was never a §14
headword, so the ledger never counted it. Today it formally enters, and its Notes cell
says exactly that (§14). Bookkeeping is a register too, and it gets the same honesty.

One forward line, and only one: next lesson finishes the set — six to ten — and fixes,
in print, a famous claim the 1.x course made about English month names. Bring your
calendar. No spoilers today.

sections.name: Vocabulary
sections.markdown:
शब्दावली — two headwords, both ledger-new; **277 → 279** (counts reconciled at review,
as always). Audio: 🔊 `planned:assets/audio/volume-2/v2c03l01-word-list.mp3` (each word
twice, three-speed passes, then the dictation track). The stems are listed in citation
dress — that is the point of them (§15).

| देवनागरी | IAST | IPA | English | हिन्दी | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| त्रि | tri | /t̪ɾi/ | three | तीन | cognate-mentioned at v1.c01.l01 and v1.c05.l03 §13 but never a headword — formally enters the ledger today (§13); dental त् + tap र्, short इ (§9) |
| चतुर् | catur | /t͡ɕɐt̪uɾ/ | four | चार | ends on bare र् — the word stops on the consonant, halanta honest (§9, §11); cognate of *quattuor* and *four* (§13); Hindi चार is its descendant |

Back on duty from Volume 1, review rows only — no re-entry to the ledger: **एक**
(eka) /eːkɐ/ "one" — एक (✓ v1.c02.l04, the course's first number word; final अ full,
never Hindi-style "ek" — §12; the shelf's honestly empty slot — §13), **द्वि**
(dvi) /d̪ʋi/ "two" — दो (✓ v1.c05.l03, the द्व ligature's word) and **पञ्च** (pañca)
/pɐɲt͡ɕɐ/ "five" — पाँच (✓ v1.c06.l01 — the ञ्च conjunct showcase, its promise kept
today).

Display-only, excluded from all counts and decks: the counting dress **एकम् · द्वे ·
त्रीणि · चत्वारि** (पञ्च keeps one shape in both jobs) — §15's business; and the digits
१–५ as content (v1.c05.l05).

Reading protocol unchanged: count the blocks, read the blocks, read the word — ए-क,
द्वि, त्रि, च-तुर्, प-ञ्च — then the roll-call (§9 drill 2), and no final sound clipped
at any speed.

sections.name: Grammar
sections.markdown:
व्याकरणम् — two dresses on one rack, and a fence with a gate marked Volume 4.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** (1) The stems एक द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च are citation names — the
> shapes the words are named by; dictionaries head five as पञ्चन् (pañcan). (2) Sanskrit
> numbers inflect for case, and एक to चतुर् for gender too; the chant एकम् द्वे त्रीणि
> चत्वारि पञ्च is the neuter counting dress — real, inflected Sanskrit, standard
> counting practice, learned whole. (3) The inflection system is honestly deferred: the
> course builds it in Volume 4; until then counting runs on the chant.
> [REF:apte1890]; [REF:whitney1889]

One drill convention, labeled as one: when a digit card goes up, this course accepts
the bare citation name — त्रि! — as the answer. That is a name-tag drill, not a full
Sanskrit word: a stem becomes a word only once it takes an ending, so a real count
closes on its last chant word — three flowers end on त्रीणि!, five on पञ्च!, which
happens to be a real form already.

### The two dresses

| Job | Shape | Where you use it |
|---|---|---|
| Citation name | एक · द्वि · त्रि · चतुर् · पञ्च | word lists, the digit-name ladder, bare digit-card answers (drill convention) |
| Counting dress | एकम् · द्वे · त्रीणि · चत्वारि · पञ्च | the chant; counting aloud while pointing |

Both rows are real Sanskrit. The left row names; the right row counts. पञ्च sits in
both unchanged — noticing that costs nothing; concluding a rule from it would cost
plenty, and we decline.

### The fence — what we are not building

अत्र त्रि फलानि?? — no. The moment a number touches a counted noun, Sanskrit wants the
number *dressed to match* — by gender, by case — and that machinery is exactly what
Volume 4 builds (the salvage map parks numeral gender at v4.c05). Until then the rule
is a fence, stated plainly: no number meets a plural noun in this course. The chant
counts while you point; the bare citation name answers a digit card; the frames stay
pause-form,
verbless or with अस्ति — safe ground, exactly as मम + family word was in Chapter 2.

sections.name: Conversation
sections.markdown:
सम्भाषणम् — one scene: माया has made digit cards; अर्जुन answers, then the garden gets
counted. Audio records into the Chapter 3 drill pack (§27). Every word is self-read.

— नमस्ते, अर्जुन! एतत् किम्?
(namaste, arjuna! etat kim?) "Greetings, Arjuna! What is this?" (She holds up the card
३.) — नमस्ते, अर्जुन! यह क्या है?

— त्रि!
(tri!) "Three!" — तीन!

— आम्! एतत् किम्?
(ām! etat kim?) "Yes! And this?" (The card ४.) — हाँ! और यह?

— चतुर्!
(catur!) "Four!" — चार!

— पुष्पम् अत्र अस्ति। पुष्पम् तत्र अपि अस्ति!
(puṣpam atra asti. puṣpam tatra api asti!) "A flower is here. And there is a flower
there too!" — फूल यहाँ है। वहाँ भी फूल है!

— एकम्… द्वे… त्रीणि… चत्वारि… पञ्च!
(ekam… dve… trīṇi… catvāri… pañca!) "One… two… three… four… five!" (He counts, one
touch per word.) — एक… दो… तीन… चार… पाँच!

— पञ्च! धन्यवादः, अर्जुन! पुनः मिलामः!
(pañca! dhanyavādaḥ, arjuna! punaḥ milāmaḥ!) "Five! Thank you, Arjuna — see you again!"
— पाँच! धन्यवाद, अर्जुन! फिर मिलेंगे!

Housekeeping: एतत् किम्? rides v2.c02.l02's pointing kit — a card is a thing, so एतत्
asks after it, and today a number answers. The chant counts while the finger points;
the last chant word, पञ्च, closes the count. And notice the question the scene never asks: "how
many?" *in Sanskrit* — that word is precisely next lesson's unlock. Pause form between
turns, one full beat, as always.

sections.name: Story
sections.markdown:
कथा — पञ्च · Five. Eight lines, told by Māyā; each line: Devanagari, IAST, English,
Hindi. The household of Chapter 2 gets counted.

1. अहम् माया। मम गृहम् अत्र अस्ति।
   (aham māyā. mama gṛham atra asti.) "I am Māyā. My home is here." — मैं माया हूँ।
   मेरा घर यहाँ है।
2. पुष्पम् अत्र अस्ति। पुष्पम् तत्र अपि अस्ति।
   (puṣpam atra asti. puṣpam tatra api asti.) "A flower is here. There is a flower
   there too." — फूल यहाँ है। वहाँ भी फूल है।
3. एकम्… द्वे… त्रीणि… चत्वारि… पञ्च!
   (ekam… dve… trīṇi… catvāri… pañca!) "One… two… three… four… five!" — एक… दो… तीन…
   चार… पाँच!
4. पञ्च!
   (pañca!) "Five!" — and she writes ५ in the dust beside the flowers. — पाँच! — और वह
   फूलों के पास ५ लिख देती है।
5. मम परिवारः अपि अत्र अस्ति।
   (mama parivāraḥ api atra asti.) "My family is here too." — मेरा परिवार भी यहाँ है।
6. माता… पिता… भ्राता अर्जुनः… भगिनी कमला… अहम् अपि!
   (mātā… pitā… bhrātā arjunaḥ… bhaginī kamalā… aham api!) "Mother… father… brother
   Arjuna… sister Kamalā… and me!" — माता… पिता… भाई अर्जुन… बहन कमला… और मैं भी!
7. एकम्… द्वे… त्रीणि… चत्वारि… पञ्च!
   (ekam… dve… trīṇi… catvāri… pañca!) "One… two… three… four… five!" (On her
   fingers.) — एक… दो… तीन… चार… पाँच!
8. मम परिवारः — पञ्च! सर्वम् शुभम्।
   (mama parivāraḥ — pañca! sarvam śubham.) "My family — five! All is well." — मेरा
   परिवार — पाँच! सब शुभ है।

The quiet craft notes: Chapter 2's household turns out to be exactly five — the
course's first census. The chant does *recitation* work in lines 3 and 7, not agreement
work — the system that would dress each number to match what it counts is Volume 4's,
and nothing here will need correcting when it arrives. The bare पञ्च! of lines 4 and 8
is the lesson's whole grammar, twice.

sections.name: Exercises
sections.markdown:
अभ्यासाः — six exercises; 2, 3, 5 and 6 are production tasks. Do them in order. Keys
live in §19's collapsed answer key — no peeking mid-run.

**अभ्यासः 1 · अङ्कनामयोजनम् (the digit-name ladder — timed).** Shuffle the five digit
cards १–५. Pass one: see the digit, say the name within a beat. Pass two, reversed:
hear the name from the audio 🔊 (or a partner), write the digit. Pass three: both
directions at natural speed; log the time. Target: ten clean answers, no translation
pause.

**अभ्यासः 2 · गणनयात्रा (the counting walk — production, spoken).** The worksheet's
picture rows: flowers, stars, trees — one to five of each. Count each row aloud with
the chant while touching each picture, then close on the last chant word: एकम्… द्वे…
त्रीणि। — त्रीणि! Then once in the real world: five real things, counted, closed on पञ्च!

**अभ्यासः 3 · श्रुतलेखनम् (dictation — production, written).** Play the dictation
track 🔊: the five stems in random order, each read twice with a writing pause, then
the chant line once. Write everything in Devanagari. Self-check against §14: चतुर् with
its halanta, पञ्च with its ञ्च stack, त्रि short. 4/5 words + chant line intact is a
pass; re-take tomorrow (§20).

**अभ्यासः 4 · अङ्कनम् (the shelf sort).** Keep or reject, one reasoning line each:
(a) "English *two* comes from Sanskrit द्वि." (b) "द्वि, Latin *duo* and English *two*
are parallel descendants of one ancestor." (c) "चतुर् and *quattuor* are cognates."
(d) "एक and *one* go back to the very same ancestral word, just as द्वि and *two* do." (e) "Hindi चार descends from Sanskrit
चतुर्." (f) "पञ्च was borrowed from Greek *pénte*." Before checking the key, find the
asymmetry: why can (e) be kept while (a) is rejected?

**अभ्यासः 5 · उत्पादनम् (produce the frames — production, written then spoken).**
Write, then say: (1) the chant, from memory, one line; (2) the answers a partner would
want for cards २, ४, ५ shown with एतत् किम्?; (3) one flower line with अस्ति and a
count closed on its last chant word, on the §6 model. Read your page aloud as one tiny presentation.

**अभ्यासः 6 · गणनम् (the recorded take — production).** One take, three rounds: (1) the
roll-call एक to पञ्च; (2) the chant on an even beat; (3) count five real objects,
pointing, and close bare. This recording is the seed of the chapter exam's counting
task (v2.c03.l05, task C) — keep it, and keep the beat.

sections.name: Quiz
sections.markdown:
प्रश्नाः — answers in the key at the end; no peeking mid-quiz.

1. The citation names of one to five, in order: (a) एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च
   (b) एक द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च (c) एक दो तीन चार पाँच (d) १ २ ३ ४ ५
2. The chant forms एकम्, द्वे, त्रीणि, चत्वारि are: (a) common mistakes for the stems
   (b) real, inflected neuter counting forms, learned whole as a chant — the system
   behind them arrives in Volume 4 (c) Hindi numbers in Sanskrit dress (d) optional
   decorations with no grammar in them
3. The stem with no clean everyday-English cognate on today's shelf: (a) द्वि (b) पञ्च
   (c) एक (d) चतुर्
4. The honest statement about त्रि and English *three*: (a) *three* descends from त्रि
   (b) त्रि descends from *three* (c) they are parallel descendants of one ancestor —
   no borrowing in any direction (d) the resemblance is coincidence
5. Hindi चार and पाँच: (a) descend from चतुर् and पञ्च — a true downward line inside
   Indo-Aryan (b) are the ancestors of the Sanskrit words (c) are unrelated to them
   (d) were borrowed into Hindi from English
6. त्रि's ledger story, honestly told: (a) it has been a headword since v1.c01.l01
   (b) it was cognate-mentioned twice before (v1.c01.l01, v1.c05.l03 §13) but enters
   the ledger as a headword only today (c) it is a review row today, like द्वि
   (d) it is display-only, like the chant forms
7. चतुर् ends: (a) in a full vowel — "catura" (b) on bare र् — the word stops on the
   consonant, as the halanta says (c) in visarga (d) in anusvāra
8. You have counted five pictured flowers. The taught answer is: (a) पञ्च! — the bare
   citation name (b) the number dressed to match the noun — machinery this course has
   not taught yet (§15's fence) (c) पाँच! (d) "panch!"

<details><summary>उत्तराणि · Answer Key</summary>

1. (b) — the stems are the citation names; (a) is the chant, (c) is Hindi, (d) is
   digits (§8, §15).
2. (b) — both rows are real; names versus counting dress (§15).
3. (c) — the honestly empty slot; reaching is how 1.x went wrong (§13).
4. (c) — siblings, no arrow — the shelf's standing law (§13).
5. (a) — descent runs downward inside Indo-Aryan, exactly like गृह → घर (§7, §14).
6. (b) — mentions are not headwords; the ledger counts honestly, 277 → 279 (§13, §14).
7. (b) — tap and stop (§10, §11 check 3). ((a) is §12's mistake 2.)
8. (a) — bare answers are the taught form; (b) names real Sanskrit the course defers —
   simplest correct beats ambitious wrong (§15); (c) and (d) are Hindi habits (§12).

**Exercise keys.** Exercise 1: १ एक · २ द्वि · ३ त्रि · ४ चतुर् · ५ पञ्च, both
directions; ten clean at a beat is the pass. Exercise 3: self-check against §14; 4/5 +
chant line intact. Exercise 4: (a) **reject** — siblings, no arrow between cousins;
(b) **keep**; (c) **keep**; (d) **reject** — they share only an ancestral root, built out with different
suffixes (§13): relatives, not a clean row, so the slot stays empty, no
reaching; (e) **keep** — a true descent line inside Indo-Aryan; (f) **reject** —
cognates, not a loan. The asymmetry: Hindi is Sanskrit's *descendant*, English is its
*sibling* — direction claims are true downward and false sideways (§7, §13). Exercises 2,
5–6 score against §6/§15: every chant word on its beat, every final sound intact,
every digit card answered with its bare name, every count closed on its last chant
word.
</details>

sections.name: Revision
sections.markdown:
पुनरावृत्तिः — one screen to remember.

> **The names:** एक · द्वि · त्रि · चतुर् · पञ्च — citation stems, the ladder's
> answers. **The chant:** एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च — the neuter counting dress,
> real and honestly deferred. **The digits:** १ २ ३ ४ ५ pair with the names at a beat.
> **The shelf:** द्वि ~ duo ~ two · त्रि ~ trēs ~ three · चतुर् ~ quattuor ~ four ·
> पञ्च ~ pénte ~ five — no arrows anywhere; एक's slot honestly empty. **The fence:** no
> number meets a plural noun before Volume 4; cards answer with the bare name — त्रि! —
> counts close on the chant word — त्रीणि! **The ledger:** two new — 277 → 279.

Spaced review (distributed practice beats cramming [REF:cepeda2006]):

- **In 1 day:** re-take the dictation (exercise 3) cold; run the ladder (exercise 1)
  once, timed; log both beside today's scores — v2.c03.l02's Station 0 then re-runs
  the chant, one pass cold, and the digit cards १–५ at speed, both directions: the
  set completes to ten tomorrow, so today's five must be automatic by then.
- **This week:** the chant once daily, pointed at real things — stairs, spoons,
  sparrows; keep the Station 0 habit warm.
- **In 1 week:** the five return inside the full ladder १–१० under the time words
  and the calendar (v2.c03.l03 onward), and the chant stands for the chapter exam's
  counting task (v2.c03.l05, task C); the shelf's honest lines — एक's empty slot and
  the chant's deferred grammar — come back in the exam quiz (Q1–Q2).

sections.name: Homework
sections.markdown:
गृहकार्यम् — about 30 minutes total.

1. **(10 min)** Finish exercises 3 and 6 if not completed in class: the dictation pass
   and the recorded counting take, kept for exam week.
2. **(10 min, real world)** Find Devanagari digits in the wild — a calendar, a
   newspaper, a wall clock — and name every १–५ you meet within a beat. Then count
   five real things at home with the chant, closing bare. If nothing printed offers
   itself, write १–५ yourself and pin them where you will pass them daily.
3. **(5 min, teach-back)** Teach someone the chant — and the honest line that comes
   with it: the stems are the numbers' names; the chant is their counting dress; the
   full system is a later volume's promise, not today's secret.
4. **(5 min, maintenance)** The family-world exam's standing item: one scene
   description from a fresh card (v2.c02.l05, task E) stays in the weekly rotation —
   run this week's now and log it.

sections.name: Teacher Notes
sections.markdown:
अध्यापकटिप्पणी

**Open with the promise, not the list.** Write पञ्च on the board and ask who can read
it (everyone — since v1.c06.l01). Then read that lesson's own line aloud: the names of
the numbers beyond पञ्च are Volume 2 Chapter 3's subject. A course that keeps its
promises on schedule earns the trust this chapter's corrections will spend.

**Timing plan (45 min):** Station 0 + prompts, scores logged (8) → the promise-kept
opening (4) → set walk-through on the digit-name cards; the त्रि bookkeeping honesty
told as a story (8) → two-dress chart: names rail, chant rail; the fence stated plainly
(6) → chant work: call-and-response on a beat, then pointing counts on the worksheet
rows (7) → ladder races in pairs, both directions, times logged (6) → word list at
three speeds; dictation launch (4) → exercises, homework, the wild-digits task (2).

**Board work:** two rails, names above (एक द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च), chant below (एकम्
द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च), the digits १–५ pinned between them — one column per number,
so the eye learns the triplet digit-name-dress as one card.

**Hold the कति line, and run the एक disappointment as a feature.** The how-many word
is next lesson's by design — let cards and fingers ask today; leaking it flattens
l02's opening. And when the shelf goes up with एक's slot empty, collect the guesses
("one? own?"), then land the point: *one* really is related to एक at the root — same
ancestor, different suffix (§13) — but it is not a clean row, so the slot stays empty;
the course could print the reach and refuses to — the exact muscle next lesson's
month-name fix will need.

**Differentiation:** Hindi speakers own the meanings for free — their work is the
finals (एक not "ek", चतुर् stopped on र्, पञ्च not पाँच) and the direction honesty:
their own दो-तीन-चार-पाँच are the descent evidence, true downward, never sideways.
Script-side learners drill त्रि and द्वि from components (v1.c05.l03–l04) before speed
work, and give the ladder extra slow passes before timing.

**What students find hard:** two shapes per number feels like double load until the
names/dress analogy lands; resisting invented agreement — park it with "Volume 4
builds exactly that"; the चतुर् full stop (English and Hindi habits both want a vowel
after it); and keeping the chant's beat honest through त्रीणि and चत्वारि — the long
vowels want to rush.

sections.name: AI Video Prompt
sections.markdown:
Lesson video, ~6 min, presenter + motion graphics.

1. **Hook (0:00–0:40):** पञ्च appears with dust blowing off it — "you have read this
   word for a volume." The digits १–५ march in beneath, each holding an empty
   name-tag. Title card: एकादिपञ्चान्ताः — One to Five.
2. **The names arrive (0:40–2:00):** card flips — each digit's name stamps on: एक,
   द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च. The चतुर् card freezes mid-flip for a halanta close-up:
   "the word stops on र्."
3. **Two dresses (2:00–3:10):** a wardrobe gag — stems wear name-tags on a rail; the
   chant forms hang below in counting aprons. A gavel labeled "RULE" descends and a
   hand parks it on a shelf marked "Volume 4".
4. **The shelf and the ladder (3:10–5:20):** four sibling pairs light up under one
   ancestor node — ties, no arrows; the एक slot stays empty ("no clean English cousin —
   and the course says so"). Then digit cards flash to a metronome; names answer
   within the beat; the reverse round writes digits as names call.
5. **Recap + CTA (5:20–6:00):** the two-dress chart assembles; the chant plays once
   over five flowers. End card: "Next: षडादिदशान्ताः — six to ten, and a famous claim
   about month names finally gets fixed."

sections.name: Voice-over Script
sections.markdown:
Narration for the lesson video (§24); Sanskrit terms carry IPA cues in [brackets] —
the narrator reads the cue, not the English spelling.

- **00:00** You have read pañca [pɐɲt͡ɕɐ] for a whole volume. Today it stops being a
  reading word and starts being a number — and it brings four friends.
- **00:40** The names: eka [eːkɐ] — say all of it, the final a is real. dvi [d̪ʋi].
  tri [t̪ɾi] — on the teeth, not the ridge. catur [t͡ɕɐt̪uɾ] — and stop: no vowel
  after the tap. pañca [pɐɲt͡ɕɐ] — a full consonant in the middle, never a nasal
  shortcut.
- **02:00** The counting dress: ekam [eːkɐm], dve [d̪ʋeː], trīṇi [t̪ɾiːɳi], catvāri
  [t͡ɕɐt̪ʋɑːɾi], pañca [pɐɲt͡ɕɐ]. Real, inflected Sanskrit — learned whole, like a
  song. The system behind it comes in Volume 4, and we say so.
- **03:10** The shelf. dvi and *two* — one ancestor. tri and *three*. catur and
  *four*. pañca and *five*. No arrows: nobody borrowed anybody's numbers. And eka
  [eːkɐ]? The slot stays empty — no clean English cousin, and honesty beats reaching.
- **04:20** The ladder: see the digit, say the name, inside one beat. When the names
  arrive without translation, you are not reciting any more — you are counting.
- **05:20** Count five real things before you sleep: ekam… dve… trīṇi… catvāri…
  pañca! Next lesson the set completes — and a famous story about your calendar gets
  told right at last.

sections.name: Reel Script
sections.markdown:
40–50 seconds, vertical, captions burned in.

- **Hook (0:00–0:07):** close-up of a hand holding the digit card ५: "You could read
  this. Could you *say* it?" Beat. "pañca [pɐɲt͡ɕɐ] — and it's cousins with *five*."
- **Demo (0:07–0:30):** the ladder at speed — digits flash, names land: १ eka! २ dvi!
  ३ tri! ४ catur! ५ pañca! Then the chant over five flowers, one touch per word:
  एकम्… द्वे… त्रीणि… चत्वारि… पञ्च!
- **Payoff (0:30–0:43):** "Learners of this course can now count to five in Sanskrit —
  and they know *two, three, four, five* are siblings of द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च, not
  borrowings. The word for one? No clean English cousin — and the course says so."
- **CTA (0:43–0:50):** "Next: षडादिदशान्ताः — six to ten, and the truth about
  November. Follow for Chapter 3." (End card: एकादिपञ्चान्ताः — one to five.)

quiz.questions_markdown:
प्रश्नाः — answers in the key at the end; no peeking mid-quiz.

1. The citation names of one to five, in order: (a) एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च
   (b) एक द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च (c) एक दो तीन चार पाँच (d) १ २ ३ ४ ५
2. The chant forms एकम्, द्वे, त्रीणि, चत्वारि are: (a) common mistakes for the stems
   (b) real, inflected neuter counting forms, learned whole as a chant — the system
   behind them arrives in Volume 4 (c) Hindi numbers in Sanskrit dress (d) optional
   decorations with no grammar in them
3. The stem with no clean everyday-English cognate on today's shelf: (a) द्वि (b) पञ्च
   (c) एक (d) चतुर्
4. The honest statement about त्रि and English *three*: (a) *three* descends from त्रि
   (b) त्रि descends from *three* (c) they are parallel descendants of one ancestor —
   no borrowing in any direction (d) the resemblance is coincidence
5. Hindi चार and पाँच: (a) descend from चतुर् and पञ्च — a true downward line inside
   Indo-Aryan (b) are the ancestors of the Sanskrit words (c) are unrelated to them
   (d) were borrowed into Hindi from English
6. त्रि's ledger story, honestly told: (a) it has been a headword since v1.c01.l01
   (b) it was cognate-mentioned twice before (v1.c01.l01, v1.c05.l03 §13) but enters
   the ledger as a headword only today (c) it is a review row today, like द्वि
   (d) it is display-only, like the chant forms
7. चतुर् ends: (a) in a full vowel — "catura" (b) on bare र् — the word stops on the
   consonant, as the halanta says (c) in visarga (d) in anusvāra
8. You have counted five pictured flowers. The taught answer is: (a) पञ्च! — the bare
   citation name (b) the number dressed to match the noun — machinery this course has
   not taught yet (§15's fence) (c) पाँच! (d) "panch!"
quiz.answer_key_markdown:
1. (b) — the stems are the citation names; (a) is the chant, (c) is Hindi, (d) is
   digits (§8, §15).
2. (b) — both rows are real; names versus counting dress (§15).
3. (c) — the honestly empty slot; reaching is how 1.x went wrong (§13).
4. (c) — siblings, no arrow — the shelf's standing law (§13).
5. (a) — descent runs downward inside Indo-Aryan, exactly like गृह → घर (§7, §14).
6. (b) — mentions are not headwords; the ledger counts honestly, 277 → 279 (§13, §14).
7. (b) — tap and stop (§10, §11 check 3). ((a) is §12's mistake 2.)
8. (a) — bare answers are the taught form; (b) names real Sanskrit the course defers —
   simplest correct beats ambitious wrong (§15); (c) and (d) are Hindi habits (§12).

**Exercise keys.** Exercise 1: १ एक · २ द्वि · ३ त्रि · ४ चतुर् · ५ पञ्च, both
directions; ten clean at a beat is the pass. Exercise 3: self-check against §14; 4/5 +
chant line intact. Exercise 4: (a) **reject** — siblings, no arrow between cousins;
(b) **keep**; (c) **keep**; (d) **reject** — they share only an ancestral root, built out with different
suffixes (§13): relatives, not a clean row, so the slot stays empty, no
reaching; (e) **keep** — a true descent line inside Indo-Aryan; (f) **reject** —
cognates, not a loan. The asymmetry: Hindi is Sanskrit's *descendant*, English is its
*sibling* — direction claims are true downward and false sideways (§7, §13). Exercises 2,
5–6 score against §6/§15: every chant word on its beat, every final sound intact,
every digit card answered with its bare name, every count closed on its last chant
word.

registers.text: The stems एक, द्वि, त्रि, चतुर्, पञ्च are the numbers' citation names — the shapes this course teaches first and dictionaries list (पञ्च is headed by its full stem पञ्चन् (pañcan), whose final न् drops in compounds and in the counting form). In running Sanskrit, numbers *inflect*: they change dress by gender and case. The neuter counting recitation — एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च — is standard practice, real inflected Sanskrit learned whole. [REF:apte1890]; [REF:whitney1889]

Number names are the textbook case for automaticity: a digit's name must arrive without translation, or counting stays a classroom trick. Timed retrieval of small chunks — today's beat-paced digit-name ladder — is the fluency strand doing exactly its job. [REF:nation2013]

Spaced retrieval beats massed re-study; today's Station 0 is v2.c02.l05's +1-week interval landing on schedule, and this lesson sets its own +1-day and +1-week re-runs before it ends (§20). [REF:cepeda2006] [REF:roediger2006]

Numerals are among the most stable items of basic vocabulary — rarely borrowed, slowly replaced. That stability is why they preserve the systematic sound-correspondences that serve as evidence of shared descent, and why the numeral set is a classic showcase of the Indo-European family's unity. [REF:mallory2006]

द्वि ~ Latin *duo* ~ English *two* · त्रि ~ Latin *trēs* ~ English *three* · चतुर् ~ Latin *quattuor* ~ English *four* · पञ्च ~ Greek *pénte* ~ English *five* — parallel descendants of the Proto-Indo-European numerals, among the most stable words in the family. No borrowing happened in any direction: nobody's "three" came from anybody else's. [REF:mallory2006]; [REF:burrow2001]

(1) The stems एक द्वि त्रि चतुर् पञ्च are citation names — the shapes the words are named by; dictionaries head five as पञ्चन् (pañcan). (2) Sanskrit numbers inflect for case, and एक to चतुर् for gender too; the chant एकम् द्वे त्रीणि चत्वारि पञ्च is the neuter counting dress — real, inflected Sanskrit, standard counting practice, learned whole. (3) The inflection system is honestly deferred: the course builds it in Volume 4; until then counting runs on the chant. [REF:apte1890]; [REF:whitney1889]
